destination.name: Ecuador and the Galápagos
destination.pitch: Two weeks that are really one archipelago plus a short mainland prologue, and the honest arithmetic is that the islands will take about two thirds of your money before you have bought a single meal.

because.nature: Animals that were never hunted and do not move when you approach, at a density no mainland park can match, plus 370 bird species in the cloud forest two hours from the capital.
because.exploration: Four distinct worlds inside one country: a 2,850 metre colonial capital, a wet Andean cloud forest, volcanic islands and the water between them.
because.food: Quito has a genuinely good restaurant scene for the money, and Galápagos food is limited, flown in and expensive, with the honourable exception of the fish kiosks in Puerto Ayora.
because.relaxation: Puerto Villamil on Isabela is the one place in the islands where nothing is scheduled and the beach is empty, which is the right way to spend your middle days.
because.culture: The islands' human history of failed colonies, penal settlements and a 1930s murder mystery is stranger than the wildlife, and the interpretation centre on San Cristóbal tells it straight.
because.adventure: Sierra Negra's caldera rim, the Los Túneles lava arches and the channel snorkel at León Dormido are all real days out, and all of them get cancelled by weather.
because.city: Quito's old town is the best preserved colonial centre in the Americas and it is worth two days, not five.

destination.caveat: The Galápagos costs money twice: the national park fee doubled to USD 200 per foreign adult in August 2024 and is still cash on arrival, the INGALA transit card is another USD 20, and the Quito to Baltra or San Cristóbal flight is a separate ticket of roughly USD 350 to 500 return that is not in the Put together for you just now from what I know, rather than checked against today's opening times. Worth confirming anything you're pinning the trip on.

cities.name: Quito
cities.base: La Floresta or the quieter edge of La Mariscal. You get the good restaurants, safe streets at night and a ten dollar taxi to the old town. Sleeping inside the Centro Histórico is atmospheric and dead

cities.name: Mindo
cities.base: Either in Mindo village itself, which is four streets and walkable to the chocolate tour and the buses, or a lodge on the Nambillo road if birds are the point and you want feeders outside the window.

cities.name: Santa Cruz
cities.base: Puerto Ayora, and within it the blocks between Avenida Charles Darwin and Baltra Avenue. Everything leaves from the main pier, the Tortuga Bay gate is a fifteen minute walk and the day-boat agencies a

cities.name: Isabela
cities.base: Puerto Villamil, on or just behind the beach road. The village is sand streets and about 2,500 people, the boat dock is a ten minute walk east and everything else is a bike ride west. The speedboat fr

cities.name: San Cristóbal
cities.base: Puerto Baquerizo Moreno, along or one street back from the Malecón Charles Darwin. The airport is a five minute taxi from the middle of town, which makes this the sane place to spend your last island

cities.name: Floreana
cities.base: You do not sleep here on a twelve day trip. Puerto Velasco Ibarra has around 150 residents and a handful of rooms, the ferry runs on a schedule that traps you for a night, and the sites worth the cros

outings.name: the Quito old town walk
outings.why: Plaza Grande, La Compañía, San Francisco, Casa del Alabado and the Basílica towers, on foot, in one loop. The hard part is not the distance, it is 2,850 metres of altitude on a first or second day, so go slowly and stop for lunch at the Mer
outings.fallback: Drop the Basílica towers and the Panecillo and keep it to the four blocks around Plaza Grande.

outings.name: the TelefériQo and Cruz Loma
outings.why: Cable car from 3,000 to 3,945 metres, then an hour of ridge walking on the Pichincha flank. Do it on day three, not day one, and be up there before 10:00 because the cloud arrives with the afternoon.
outings.season: All year, clearest June to September
outings.fallback: Parque Itchimbía and Café Mosaico for the same view at a third of the altitude.

outings.name: Rucu Pichincha
outings.why: From the top cable car station to a 4,696 metre summit, with a loose scrambling headwall in the last 200 metres. This is a serious altitude day and only makes sense late in a Quito stay, never before the Galápagos leg.
outings.season: All year, driest June to September
outings.fallback: Walk to the cross above the cable car station and turn back at the saddle.

outings.name: the Santuario de Cascadas circuit
outings.why: Taxi to the tarabita, cross the gorge in the cable car, then walk a loop taking in Nambillo, Reina and four smaller falls. Trails are mud under cloud forest, the last tarabita back is around 16:30, and you will get wet either from the falls
outings.season: All year, driest June to September
outings.fallback: The tarabita and Cascada Nambillo alone, about two hours.

outings.name: the Paz de las Aves dawn lek
outings.why: Leave at 04:30 for the cock-of-the-rock lek at first light, then follow Angel Paz around the farm while he calls antpittas in by name. Steep wet trails in the dark and the single best bird morning in Ecuador outside the Amazon.
outings.fallback: The hummingbird feeders on the Mindo Gardens road, over coffee, at a civilised hour.

outings.name: the Tortuga Bay walk
outings.why: A 2.5 km paved path from the gate on the edge of Puerto Ayora out to Playa Brava, then twenty minutes further to the mangrove lagoon at Playa Mansa where the water is flat and the marine iguanas pile up. Free, unguided, no shade on the path
outings.fallback: Water taxi across to Playa de los Alemanes and Las Grietas instead, about two hours.

outings.name: the Santa Cruz highlands and El Chato
outings.why: Los Gemelos, a lava tunnel and wild giant tortoises on farmland at El Chato, done by hired taxi for around USD 40 to 60 for the vehicle. Rubber boots are lent at the gate and the tortoises are easiest to find December to May when the highla
outings.season: All year, best December to May
outings.fallback: Bus to Santa Rosa and rent a bike, which turns it into a half day on El Chato only.

outings.name: North Seymour
outings.why: A day boat from the Itabaca channel to an uninhabited islet with frigatebird and blue-footed booby colonies nesting at your feet, usually paired with a snorkel and Las Bachas beach. Licensed naturalist guide required, fixed trail, and the c
outings.season: All year, booby courtship strongest May to November
outings.fallback: The Santa Cruz highlands run, which needs no boat and no swell.

outings.name: Bartolomé
outings.why: Two hours each way by boat, a 372 step boardwalk to the lookout over Pinnacle Rock, and a snorkel where penguins sometimes turn up. It is the postcard view of the archipelago and it is a very long day for one hour of walking.
outings.season: All year, seas roughest July to October
outings.fallback: Las Grietas and the fish market, and save the money.

outings.name: the Floreana day tour
outings.why: Two hours by speedboat each way for Post Office Bay, the highlands at Asilo de la Paz and a snorkel, with the Baroness murder story running through all of it. Around USD 150 to 200, guide included and compulsory, and the crossing is the rou
outings.season: All year, calmest December to May
outings.fallback: Nothing on Floreana is doable without the boat, so switch the day to North Seymour or the highlands.

outings.name: Las Tintoreras
outings.why: A ten minute boat hop to a lava islet with a narrow channel where white-tipped reef sharks stack up to rest, then a snorkel with sea lions, turtles and penguins. Licensed guide required, about USD 40 to 50, and the snorkel is the better hal
outings.fallback: Concha de Perla at high tide, free, which has most of the same animals without the sharks.

outings.name: Los Túneles
outings.why: An hour by boat down the south coast to collapsed lava arches in waist-deep clear water, with reef sharks under the ledges, seahorses in the mangrove and often penguins. The entry crosses a surf break, so the tour gets cancelled outright in
outings.season: All year, most often cancelled July to October
outings.fallback: Las Tintoreras in the morning and the Muro de las Lágrimas ride in the afternoon.

outings.name: Sierra Negra and Volcán Chico
outings.why: A 45 minute ride up to the trailhead, then roughly 16 km return along the caldera rim and out across the fumaroles and oxidised rock of Volcán Chico. Compulsory licensed guide, a 07:30 start, no shade, and the rim is frequently inside a clo
outings.season: All year, clearest June to December
outings.fallback: Turn back at the first rim viewpoint, which halves it to about four hours.

outings.name: the Muro de las Lágrimas ride
outings.why: Six kilometres west on a rented bike along a flat sand and gravel track, stopping at tortoise paths, lookouts and empty beaches, ending at a wall built by prison labour in the 1940s. Bikes are about USD 10 a day and there is no water or sha
outings.fallback: Walk the Humedales boardwalk to the Tupiza breeding centre and back, about ninety minutes.

outings.name: León Dormido
outings.why: Two hours out to a split tuff cone and a snorkel through the channel between the two halves, with Galápagos sharks, turtles and sometimes hammerheads. Boat and licensed guide only, the water is cold and deep with no bottom in sight, and it
outings.season: All year, hammerheads most likely June to November
outings.fallback: Snorkel at Tijeretas cove and walk the cliff path to Punta Carola.

outings.name: the San Cristóbal highlands run
outings.why: A hired taxi over the island to El Junco crater lake, La Galapaguera at Cerro Colorado and down to the beach at Puerto Chino, about USD 60 to 80 for the car for the day. El Junco sits in drizzle most mornings and Puerto Chino has no facilit
outings.fallback: La Lobería and the cliff trail south of it, on foot, half a day.

places.name: Basílica del Voto Nacional
places.note: Entry to the nave is about USD 2 and the towers cost another 2 to 3 on top, paid separately at a second desk. The tower route ends on open plank walkways and two near vertical ladders, and at 2,850 metres you will be out of breath at the top.

places.name: Iglesia de la Compañía de Jesús
places.note: The gold leaf interior is the best single room in Quito and photography inside is not allowed. Hours shift for mass and the ticket office closes before the church does, so go in the morning rather than after lunch.

places.name: Plaza and Convento de San Francisco
places.note: The plaza is free and the convent museum charges a small fee for the choir loft and the Franciscan art collection. The museum closes earlier on Sundays than the church does.

places.name: Museo Casa del Alabado
places.note: Pre-Columbian ceramics arranged by cosmology rather than by date, in a restored colonial house two minutes from San Francisco. It is the one Quito museum that rewards a slow hour.

places.name: Museo de la Ciudad
places.note: Quito's story told inside the old San Juan de Dios hospital, which is half the interest. Closed Mondays like most municipal museums here.

places.name: Capilla del Hombre and Museo Guayasamín
places.note: One ticket covers the chapel and the painter's house next door, and the house is the better half. Closed Mondays, and the hillside setting gives you the valley view Quito rarely hands out for free.

places.name: TelefériQo to Cruz Loma
places.note: The cable car lifts you from 3,000 to 3,945 metres in twenty minutes, which is exactly the wrong thing to do on your first day. Go on day two or three, go early before the cloud builds, and take a jacket.

places.name: Rucu Pichincha summit trail
places.note: From the top cable car station it is roughly 5 km each way to a 4,696 metre summit with a scrambly final headwall. Only attempt this after several days at altitude, and turn around if cloud closes in because the path is easy to lose.

places.name: Mercado Central
places.note: Second floor comedores do hornado, seco de chivo and fruit juices for a few dollars each. Come at noon when the turnover is fast, and pick a stall with a queue of office workers.

places.name: Calle La Ronda
places.note: A restored colonial lane that is quiet on weeknights and full of canelazo and live music Thursday to Saturday. Worth an hour on a Friday, worth nothing on a Tuesday.

places.name: Urko Cocina Local
places.note: A tasting menu built on Ecuadorian altitude ingredients, from the coast up to the páramo, and the cheapest serious restaurant meal of this trip by a distance. Book several days ahead.

places.name: Zazu
places.note: The reliable grown-up dinner in Quito, Peruvian influenced, with the deepest wine list in the city. Less inventive than Urko and easier to get into.

places.name: Café Mosaico
places.note: The view over the old town at dusk is the reason, the Greek-Ecuadorian menu is not. Go for a drink at 17:30, not for dinner, and reserve a terrace table.

places.name: Ciudad Mitad del Mundo
places.note: The painted line is around 240 metres off the actual equator, the complex is a shopping precinct with a monument in it, and it eats four hours of a short Quito stay including traffic. Skip it and spend the morning in the old town instead.

places.name: The tarabita and the Santuario de Cascadas circuit
places.note: A hand-built cable car crosses the Nambillo gorge and drops you at a trail network with six or seven waterfalls on it. Entry runs about USD 5 plus the tarabita, the loops take 20 to 90 minutes each, and the last car back is around 16:30.

places.name: Cascada Nambillo
places.note: The biggest fall on the circuit, with a pool you can swim in if you do not mind cold water. The last stretch is steep mud after rain, which in a cloud forest is most days.

places.name: Cascada Reina
places.note: Quieter than Nambillo and reached on the same ticket, about 25 minutes further along the ridge trail. Go here if a tour bus has just unloaded at the main falls.

places.name: Mariposas de Mindo
places.note: Around USD 8.50 for a walk-in butterfly house with a breeding room where you can watch them emerge. Go before 11:00 when the sun is on the flight house and the butterflies are actually flying.

places.name: El Quetzal de Mindo chocolate tour
places.note: Bean to bar, roasted and ground on site, about USD 10 and it ends with a brownie and tasting. Tours run at set times through the day, so ask at the door the evening before.

places.name: The hummingbird feeders at Mindo Gardens road
places.note: Several small gardens on the road out of town charge a few dollars to sit with a coffee while fifteen species work the feeders. Booted racket-tail and violet-tailed sylph are the ones people come for.

places.name: Refugio Paz de las Aves
places.note: A farmer who learned to call antpittas by name, plus a cock-of-the-rock lek at first light. You leave Mindo around 04:30 and it is the single best wildlife morning on the Ecuadorian mainland.

places.name: Tubing the Río Mindo
places.note: Lashed inner tubes, two guides and 30 to 45 minutes of class two water for under USD 10. Fun, wet, and not a serious rafting trip.

places.name: Mindo Canopy Adventure
places.note: Ten or so zip lines strung across the cloud forest, around USD 20 to 25 for the full circuit. It is a generic canopy zip course that happens to be sited in a cloud forest, you see nothing alive from it, and on a two night Mindo stop it costs you a morning you should spend on the waterfall trails or

places.name: The frog concert at Mindo Lago
places.note: A guided night walk around a pond listening to and spotting tree frogs, starting around 18:30 and costing about USD 6. Simple and genuinely good if it has not rained too hard.

places.name: Tortuga Bay
places.note: A 2.5 km paved path from the edge of town to Playa Brava, then 20 minutes more to the calm lagoon at Playa Mansa. You sign in and out at the gate, it is free, and you can do it without a guide, which is rare here.

places.name: Charles Darwin Research Station
places.note: The exhibition hall is free and open 08:00 to 18:00, and Lonesome George is in it. The Fausto Llerena tortoise breeding pens next door keep shorter split hours and a local guide fee of around USD 10 is charged at that entrance.

places.name: Las Grietas
places.note: A flooded fissure between two lava walls, reached by a USD 1 water taxi and then a 20 minute walk over rough lava. Around USD 10 to enter, and the last entry is mid afternoon.

places.name: Playa de los Alemanes
places.note: A small sheltered beach on the way to Las Grietas, five minutes from the water taxi landing. Good for an hour of flat water when Tortuga Bay's surf side is too rough.

places.name: The Puerto Ayora fish market
places.note: Pelicans and a resident sea lion stand at the counter waiting for scraps while the day's catch is filleted. It happens between roughly 07:00 and 11:00 and is over quickly.

places.name: Calle de los Kioscos on Charles Binford
places.note: Open-air stalls that close the street at dusk and grill whole fish, lobster tail in season and ceviche for USD 5 to 15. This is where people who live here eat.

places.name: Isla Grill
places.note: Whole grilled corvina with cilantro-lime butter, generous enough to split. A sit-down step up from the kiosks without the marina prices.

places.name: Lava Java
places.note: Espresso and a large breakfast on the main street, open early enough to feed you before a 07:00 boat. Coffee on the islands is otherwise mostly bad.

places.name: Los Gemelos
places.note: Two collapsed magma chambers either side of the Baltra road, ringed by Scalesia forest where vermilion flycatchers are common. Fifteen minutes at each if you walk the short rim trails.

places.name: El Chato tortoise reserve
places.note: Wild giant tortoises on private farmland in the humid highlands, about USD 10 with rubber boots lent at the gate. This is the place to see them out of a pen and they are easiest to find in the wet months.

places.name: The lava tunnels at Bellavista
places.note: A lit lava tube you walk through for a few hundred metres, usually bundled with El Chato. Low ceiling in places and the floor is wet.

places.name: Playa El Garrapatero
places.note: A 45 minute taxi then a 15 minute trail to a wide beach with a flamingo lagoon behind it. Fewer people than Tortuga Bay because you have to pay for the ride, and the taxi has to wait for you.

places.name: The Media Luna and Cerro Crocker trail
places.note: A muddy open path up through miconia scrub towards the island's high point, starting above Bellavista. It is free and unguided to Media Luna, often in cloud, and the views are a lottery.

places.name: Sierra Negra and Volcán Chico
places.note: Roughly 16 km return along the rim of one of the widest calderas on earth and out onto the orange fumarole ground at Volcán Chico. A licensed guide is compulsory, tours leave Puerto Villamil around 07:30, and the rim is often socked in by 11:00.

places.name: Los Túneles at Cabo Rosa
places.note: Collapsed lava arches in shallow clear water, with white-tipped reef sharks under the ledges, seahorses and often penguins. The boat ride out crosses a surf break that gets cancelled in swell, and it cannot be done without a licensed guide and a permitted boat.

places.name: Las Tintoreras
places.note: A short boat hop to a lava islet with a channel where reef sharks rest, then a snorkel with sea lions and penguins. Guide compulsory, roughly two and a half hours, and the best half is the snorkel not the walk.

places.name: Concha de Perla
places.note: A mangrove boardwalk to a sheltered natural pool where sea lions, turtles and rays come in. Free, no guide needed, and much better at high tide because it drains to knee depth at low water.

places.name: Muro de las Lágrimas
places.note: A 6 km ride or walk west from town to a wall built by penal colony prisoners in the 1940s, with tortoise paths, lookouts and beaches strung along the way. Bikes rent for about USD 10 a day, take water because there is none out there.

places.name: Centro de Crianza Arnaldo Tupiza
places.note: The island's tortoise breeding centre, free, reached over the wetland boardwalk from town. Isabela's five volcanoes each have their own tortoise lineage and this is where you see the difference.

places.name: The Humedales boardwalk
places.note: A raised boardwalk through brackish lagoons and mangrove linking town to the breeding centre, with Poza Redonda and Playa del Amor off it. Almost nobody walks it and the birding is good at dusk.

places.name: Poza de los Flamencos
places.note: A brackish lagoon on the edge of town with a handful of Galápagos flamingos, visible from the road. Worth ten minutes on the way past, not a trip in itself.

places.name: Playa Grande at Puerto Villamil
places.note: Three kilometres of soft sand straight off the main street, with a surf break at the western end. The best plain beach in the inhabited Galápagos and hardly anyone is on it.

places.name: Coco Surf
places.note: Fish, burgers and a set menu on a sand floor a block from the beach. Isabela has maybe a dozen places to eat and this is the one that is consistently open and consistently fine.

places.name: Bar de Beto
places.note: A driftwood bar with its feet in the sand and the whole island's evening in it. Closes early by mainland standards because the boats leave at dawn.

places.name: Centro de Interpretación
places.note: Free, well made, and the only place in the islands that tells the human history honestly, including the failed colonies and the penal settlement. Do it on your first afternoon so the rest of the week makes sense.

places.name: Cerro Tijeretas
places.note: A paved trail behind the interpretation centre to a frigatebird nesting hill and a cove you can snorkel from. Free, unguided, about an hour up and back, and the light is best early.

places.name: Playa Mann
places.note: A town beach where sea lions sleep on the sand and you are required to keep two metres away, which they ignore. Sunset here is the standard evening in Puerto Baquerizo.

places.name: La Lobería
places.note: A rocky sea lion colony 20 minutes' walk or a USD 3 taxi from town, with a cliff trail beyond it and marine iguanas everywhere. Surf can be heavy, so check before you swim.

places.name: Punta Carola
places.note: The surf beach past Playa Mann, reached on the same path, with the best sunset angle on the island. Rip currents are real here.

places.name: León Dormido
places.note: A 148 metre tuff cone split by a channel you snorkel through, with Galápagos sharks and, if you are lucky, hammerheads. Boat and licensed guide only, around two hours each way, and the water in the channel is cold and deep with nothing under you.

places.name: Laguna El Junco
places.note: A crater lake at about 700 metres, one of the few permanent freshwater bodies in the archipelago, with a 20 minute stepped loop around the rim. It is in cloud and drizzle more often than not, so bring a shell.

places.name: La Galapaguera de Cerro Colorado
places.note: A semi-wild tortoise reserve on the road to the southeast coast, with a shaded loop trail through the enclosure. Usually visited as the middle stop of the highlands taxi run.

places.name: Puerto Chino
places.note: A ten minute trail over a ridge drops onto a small white beach with boobies on the headland and no facilities at all. Your taxi waits at the top, so agree the time before you walk down.

places.name: Muyu
places.note: The best cooking on the island, seafood led, on the malecón with tables outside. Small, so book or turn up before 19:00.

places.name: The Malecón Charles Darwin at dusk
places.note: Sea lions take the benches, the pier and occasionally the moored boats, and the whole town walks up and down. Free, and the single most Galápagos thing in any of the port towns.

places.name: Post Office Bay
places.note: A barrel on a beach that whalers used as a mail drop from 1793, where you leave a postcard and hand-deliver one addressed near home. The barrel is a replica and the ritual is the point.

places.name: Asilo de la Paz
places.note: The freshwater spring and pirate caves that made settlement possible here, plus a tortoise enclosure, up in the green highlands. The walk up is steep and hot and a guide takes you through the Wittmer and Baroness story on the way.

places.name: Mirador de la Baronesa
places.note: The lookout where the self-styled Baroness of Floreana watched for boats before she vanished in 1934. A short lava climb for a view over the bay, and the story is better than the view.

places.name: Punta Cormorant
places.note: An olive-green sand beach, a brackish lagoon with flamingos, and a flour-sand turtle nesting beach on the far side where swimming is banned. Licensed guide required and the trail is fixed, you do not wander.

places.name: Corona del Diablo
places.note: A sunken volcanic cone whose rim breaks the surface, with the strongest current of any snorkel site you will do on this trip. Sharks, rays and big schools, entry and exit from the boat only, and it is closed to visitors when the swell is up.

places.name: Champion Islet
places.note: A snorkel drift along a small islet that holds one of the last populations of the Floreana mockingbird, which you will see only from the water. Permitted boats only and no landing is allowed.

places.name: Playa Negra
places.note: The black sand beach in front of the village, where the day boats wait and rays cruise the shallows. This is the only part of Floreana that feels lived in.

places.name: La Lobería de Floreana
places.note: A short walk south of the village to a rocky shore with sea lions, turtles in the shallows and no shade. Easy, free and usually empty.

places.name: Hotel Wittmer at Playa Negra
places.note: Run by the descendants of the family that settled Floreana in 1932 and outlived everyone else in the story. Lunch is simple and the connection to the island's strangest chapter is the reason to sit down.
